name: Fasoracetam

lead: Fasoracetam is a racetam discovered by Nippon Shinyaku in the late 1980s. It was tested for vascular dementia, then repurposed for ADHD and a genetic syndrome, and is now sold online as a nootropic that users take for focus and attention.
It appears to modulate metabotropic glutamate receptors. Human research is limited to small trials. Its role in the nootropic stack is mental performance.

paras: It is taken as a nootropic supplement, typically in racetam-style stacks for study and work.
It is not approved for any use. Side-effect information is limited to small trials.

angle.text: Fasoracetam is a racetam that nootropic users take for focus and attention, following its trials in ADHD. It sits in the nootropic stack for better mental performance.

lead: Fasoracetam is an experimental racetam-class drug discovered by Nippon Shinyaku in the late 1980s and never marketed. It was tested for vascular dementia, then repurposed for ADHD and later other conditions.[1] It appears to modulate metabotropic glutamate receptors.[1]
It is sold online as a nootropic. Sources reviewed do not connect it to physical appearance.
infobox: Investigational; Schedule 4 in Australia; not FDA-approved[1]

paras: Nippon Shinyaku's phase 3 trials in vascular dementia did not show sufficient efficacy.[1] A 2018 open-label, single-blind study in 30 adolescents with ADHD carrying mGluR network gene variants reported safety, pharmacokinetic and response data.[2] A 2019 systematic review of novel ADHD compounds covered the drug.[3] A phase 2 trial in children and adolescents with 22q11 deletion syndrome was completed in 2022 (n=37).[4]
It is orally bioavailable in animals with an elimination half-life of about 4 to 6.5 hours and is excreted mostly unchanged. Cognitive benefits were observed in rodent studies.[1]

timeline.event: Study in adolescents with ADHD and mGluR variants published.[2]
Phase 2 trial in 22q11 deletion syndrome started.[4]
